claim: Germ cells in many organisms develop as a 'cyst' of interconnected cells.
source: Two broadly known characteristics of germ cells in many organisms are their development as a 'cyst' of interconnected cells and their high sensitivity to DNA damage.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on germ cell development across species.

claim: Germ cells exhibit high sensitivity to DNA damage.
source: Two broadly known characteristics of germ cells in many organisms are their development as a 'cyst' of interconnected cells and their high sensitivity to DNA damage.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature and is presented as established knowledge.

claim: In the Drosophila testis, connectivity serves as a mechanism that confers to spermatogonia a high sensitivity to DNA damage.
source: Here we provide evidence that in the Drosophila testis, connectivity serves as a mechanism that confers to spermatogonia a high sensitivity to DNA damage.
evidence: This is the main claim of the study, supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: All spermatogonia within a cyst die synchronously even when only a subset of them exhibit detectable DNA damage.
source: We show that all spermatogonia within a cyst die synchronously even when only a subset of them exhibit detectable DNA damage.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations using γ-H2Av and Lysotracker staining shown in Figure 2.

claim: Mutants of the fusome compromise synchronous spermatogonial death and reduce overall germ cell death.
source: Mutants of the fusome, an organelle that is known to facilitate intracyst communication, compromise synchronous spermatogonial death and reduces overall germ cell death.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from α-spectrin RNAi and hts mutants shown in Figure 3.

claim: A death-promoting signal is shared within the cyst, leading to death of the entire cyst.
source: Our data indicate that a death-promoting signal is shared within the cyst, leading to death of the entire cyst.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observations of synchronized death and fusome mutant phenotypes.

claim: Intercellular connectivity supported by the fusome uniquely increases the sensitivity of the germline to DNA damage.
source: Taken together, we propose that intercellular connectivity supported by the fusome uniquely increases the sensitivity of the germline to DNA damage, thereby protecting the integrity of gamete genomes that are passed on to the next generation.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, based on the integration of all experimental findings.

claim: Germ cells divide with incomplete cytokinesis that results in interconnected cells with shared cytoplasm in many organisms from insects to humans.
source: In many organisms from insects to humans, germ cells divide with incomplete cytokinesis that results in interconnected cells with shared cytoplasm, leading to cyst formation
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on germ cell development.

claim: Intercellular connectivity is critical for oocyte specification in oogenesis of many species from flies to mammals.
source: During oogenesis of many species from flies to mammals, this intercellular connectivity is critical for the process of oocyte specification, allowing only some of the developing germ cells to become oocytes while the others adopt a supportive role
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on oogenesis.

claim: In the Drosophila ovary, four rounds of germ cell divisions with incomplete cytokinesis results in a cyst of 16 interconnected germ cells.
source: For example, in the Drosophila ovary, four rounds of germ cell divisions with incomplete cytokinesis results in a cyst of 16 interconnected germ cells, where only one becomes an oocyte while the remaining 15 germ cells become nurse cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila oogenesis, supported by citations.

claim: In Drosophila oogenesis, only one of 16 interconnected germ cells becomes an oocyte while the remaining 15 become nurse cells.
source: in the Drosophila ovary, four rounds of germ cell divisions with incomplete cytokinesis results in a cyst of 16 interconnected germ cells, where only one becomes an oocyte while the remaining 15 germ cells become nurse cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila oogenesis, supported by citations.

claim: Nurse cells support oocyte development by providing their cytoplasmic contents to oocytes via intercellular trafficking.
source: During this process, nurse cells support oocyte development by providing their cytoplasmic contents to oocytes via intercellular trafficking
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on Drosophila oogenesis.

claim: In spermatogenesis, all germ cells within a cyst are considered to be equivalent and become mature gametes.
source: In contrast to oogenesis, where cytoplasmic connectivity has a clear developmental role in oocyte development, spermatogenesis is a process where all germ cells within a cyst are considered to be equivalent and become mature gametes
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on spermatogenesis.

claim: Intercellular connectivity is widely observed in spermatogenesis in a broad range of organisms.
source: Despite the lack of a 'nursing mechanism' during spermatogenesis, intercellular connectivity is widely observed in spermatogenesis in a broad range of organisms
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: A function for germ cell connectivity has been proposed in post-meiotic spermatids in complementing haploid genomes.
source: While a function for this connectivity has been proposed in post-meiotic spermatids in complementing haploid genomes (Braun et al., 1989), the biological significance of male germ cell connectivity during pre-meiotic stages of spermatogenesis remains unknown.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The biological significance of male germ cell connectivity during pre-meiotic stages of spermatogenesis remains unknown.
source: the biological significance of male germ cell connectivity during pre-meiotic stages of spermatogenesis remains unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: The germline exhibits extreme sensitivity to DNA damage compared to the soma.
source: Another well-known characteristic of the germline is its extreme sensitivity to DNA damage compared to the soma, with clinical interventions such as radiation or chemotherapy often resulting in impaired fertility
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on clinical observations.

claim: Radiation or chemotherapy often results in impaired fertility.
source: with clinical interventions such as radiation or chemotherapy often resulting in impaired fertility
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on clinical observations.

claim: The high sensitivity of the germline to DNA damage is postulated to be part of a quality control mechanism for the germ cell genome.
source: It has been postulated that the high sensitivity of the germline to DNA damage is part of a quality control mechanism for the germ cell genome, which is passed onto the next generation
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The means by which the germline achieves high sensitivity to DNA damage remains unclear.
source: However, the means by which the germline achieves such a high sensitivity to DNA damage remains unclear.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: An entire spermatogonial cyst undergoes synchronized cell death as a unit even when only a subset of spermatogonia within the cyst exhibit detectable DNA damage.
source: We show that an entire SG cyst undergoes synchronized cell death as a unit even when only a subset of SGs within the cyst exhibit detectable DNA damage.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Disruption of the fusome compromises synchronized germ cell death within a cyst in response to DNA damage.
source: Disruption of the fusome, a germline-specific organelle that facilitates communication amongst germ cells within a cyst (de Cuevas et al., 1997), compromises synchronized germ cell death within a cyst in response to DNA damage.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from fusome mutants shown in Figure 3.

claim: The fusome is a germline-specific organelle that facilitates communication amongst germ cells within a cyst.
source: the fusome, a germline-specific organelle that facilitates communication amongst germ cells within a cyst
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The sensitivity of a germ cell cyst to DNA damage increases as the number of interconnected germ cells within increases.
source: The sensitivity of a germ cell cyst to DNA damage increases as the number of interconnected germ cells within increases, demonstrating that connectivity serves as a mechanism to confer higher sensitivity to DNA damage.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Germ cell cyst formation serves as a mechanism to increase the sensitivity of genome surveillance.
source: Taken together, we propose that germ cell cyst formation serves as a mechanism to increase the sensitivity of genome surveillance, ensuring the quality of the genome that is passed onto the next generation.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, based on the integration of all experimental findings.

claim: The Drosophila testis serves as an excellent model to study germ cell development owing to its well-defined spatiotemporal organization.
source: The Drosophila testis serves as an excellent model to study germ cell development owing to its well-defined spatiotemporal organization, with spermatogenesis proceeding from the apical tip down the length of the testis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Drosophila testis as a model system.

claim: In the Drosophila testis, spermatogenesis proceeds from the apical tip down the length of the testis.
source: with spermatogenesis proceeding from the apical tip down the length of the testis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila spermatogenesis.

claim: Germline stem cells divide to produce gonialblasts, which undergo transit-amplifying divisions to become a cyst of 16 interconnected spermatogonia before entering the meiotic program as spermatocytes.
source: Germline stem cells (GSCs) divide to produce gonialblasts (GBs), which undergo transit-amplifying divisions to become a cyst of 16 interconnected spermatogonia (16-SG) before entering the meiotic program as spermatocytes (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila spermatogenesis, also illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Protein starvation induces spermatogonial death, predominantly at the early stages (~4 SG stage) of spermatogonial development.
source: In our previous study we showed that protein starvation induces SG death, predominantly at the early stages (~4 SG stage) of SG development (Yang and Yamashita, 2015) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Starvation-induced spermatogonial death is non-apoptotic.
source: Starvation-induced SG death, which itself is non-apoptotic (Yacobi-Sharon et al., 2013), is mediated by apoptosis of somatic cyst cells encapsulating the SGs
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Starvation-induced spermatogonial death is mediated by apoptosis of somatic cyst cells encapsulating the spermatogonia.
source: Starvation-induced SG death, which itself is non-apoptotic (Yacobi-Sharon et al., 2013), is mediated by apoptosis of somatic cyst cells encapsulating the SGs (Yang and Yamashita, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Cyst cell apoptosis breaks the 'blood-testis-barrier' and leads to spermatogonial death.
source: Cyst cell apoptosis breaks the 'blood-testis-barrier' and leads to SG death
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Significant spermatogonial death occurs at the 16-SG stage independent of nutrient conditions.
source: Though we noted significant SG death at the 16-SG stage in the course of our previous work, it was independent of nutrient conditions and thus was not the focus of the study (Yang and Yamashita, 2015).
evidence: This is an observation from prior work by the authors.

claim: Ionizing radiation can induce 16-SG death.
source: In search of the cause of this 16-SG death, we discovered that it can be induced by ionizing radiation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: When adult flies are exposed to ionizing radiation that causes DNA double strand breaks, a dramatic induction of spermatogonial death is observed.
source: When adult flies were exposed to ionizing radiation that causes DNA double strand breaks (DSBs), a dramatic induction of SG death was observed (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B,C.

claim: Dying spermatogonia induced by ionizing radiation can be detected by Lysotracker staining, showing characteristic acidification of the entire cell.
source: Dying SGs induced by ionizing radiation were detected by Lysotracker staining as described by previous studies, showing characteristic acidification of the entire cell
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature and experimental data.

claim: Spermatogonial death in control and irradiated flies proceeds in the same manner, where all of the spermatogonia within a cyst die simultaneously by becoming Lysotracker-positive.
source: SG death in control and irradiated flies proceeded in the same manner, where all of the SGs within a cyst die simultaneously by becoming Lysotracker-positive (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Radiation-induced spermatogonial death is not suppressed by inhibiting cyst cell apoptosis.
source: Importantly, in contrast to starvation-induced SG death which was dependent on somatic cyst cell apoptosis, radiation-induced SG death was not suppressed by inhibiting cyst cell apoptosis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), suggesting that radiation-induced SG death is a germ cell-intrinsic response.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Radiation-induced spermatogonial death is a germ cell-intrinsic response.
source: suggesting that radiation-induced SG death is a germ cell-intrinsic response.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that inhibiting cyst cell apoptosis does not suppress radiation-induced SG death.

claim: The frequency of dying spermatogonial cysts peaks around 3 to 6 hr after irradiation and decreases by 24 hr post-irradiation.
source: The frequency of dying SG cysts peaked around 3 to 6 hr after irradiation and decreased by 24 hr post-irradiation (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Ionizing radiation robustly induces cell death at the 16-SG stage, although death of other stages (2-, 4-, 8 cell SGs) is also induced.
source: Interestingly, we found that ionizing radiation robustly induces cell death at the 16-SG stage, although death of other stages (2-, 4-, 8 cell SGs) was also induced (Figure 1C and see below).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The pattern of spermatogonial death holds true regardless of the ionizing radiation dose.
source: This pattern of SG death held true regardless of the ionizing radiation dose (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Exposure to even a very low dose of ionizing radiation can dramatically induce death of 16-SGs.
source: While testing multiple doses of ionizing radiation, we noticed that exposure to even a very low dose of ionizing radiation could dramatically induce death of 16-SGs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations.

claim: The 16-SG death induced by increasing radiation is a distinctly non-linear response, quickly reaching a plateau of ~3 dying 16-SG cysts per testis.
source: By measuring dose-dependent death of 16-SGs at six hours post-irradiation, we found that the 16-SG death induced by increasing radiation was a distinctly non-linear response, quickly reaching a plateau of ~3 dying 16-SG cysts per testis (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Cell death in the wing imaginal disc follows a linear dose-response relationship where an increase in radiation results in a proportional increase in cell death.
source: In comparison, cell death in the wing imaginal disc (Figure 1—figure supplement 3) followed a linear dose-response relationship where an increase in radiation resulted in a proportional increase in cell death (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: 16-SGs demonstrate remarkable sensitivity to ionizing radiation compared to somatic cells.
source: These results demonstrate a remarkable sensitivity of 16-SGs to ionizing radiation compared to somatic cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of dose-response curves between 16-SGs and wing imaginal disc cells.

claim: DSBs result in phosphorylation of the histone H2A variant (γ-H2Av), the Drosophila equivalent of mammalian γ-H2AX.
source: DSBs result in phosphorylation of the histone H2A variant (γ-H2Av), the Drosophila equivalent of mammalian γ-H2AX, reflecting the very early cellular response to DSBs
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: γ-H2Av can be robustly detected in spermatogonia following a high dose of ionizing radiation.
source: Using an anti-γ-H2Av antibody (pS137), we confirmed that γ-H2Av can be robustly detected in SGs following a high dose of ionizing radiation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: When a low dose of ionizing radiation is used (≤100 rad), 16-SG cysts are frequently observed in which only a subset of cells within the cyst exhibit detectable γ-H2Av signal but all 16 cells are Lysotracker-positive and dying.
source: When a low dose of ionizing radiation was used (≤100 rad), we frequently observed 16-SG cysts in which only a subset of cells within the cyst exhibited detectable γ-H2Av signal but all 16 cells were Lysotracker-positive and dying (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The fraction of γ-H2Av-positive spermatogonia within each cyst increases gradually with increasing radiation dose irrespective of spermatogonial stage.
source: The fraction of γ-H2Av-positive SGs within each cyst increased gradually with increasing radiation dose irrespective of SG stage (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2), consistent with the linear nature in which ionizing radiation damages DNA molecules
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The increase in γ-H2Av-positive spermatogonia with increasing radiation dose is consistent with the linear nature in which ionizing radiation damages DNA molecules.
source: consistent with the linear nature in which ionizing radiation damages DNA molecules (Ulsh, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature on radiation biology.

claim: Spermatogonia within a cyst are always either all Lysotracker-positive or -negative.
source: However, Lysotracker staining showed that SGs within a cyst were always either all Lysotracker-positive or -negative (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 2C.

claim: While DNA damage is induced in individual spermatogonia within a cyst proportional to the dose of radiation, cell death is induced in all of the spermatogonia within the entire cyst.
source: These results suggest that while DNA damage is induced in individual SGs within a cyst proportional to the dose of radiation, cell death is induced in all of the SGs within the entire cyst, leading to elevated SG death that follows a non-linear response with increasing dose.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of γ-H2Av and Lysotracker staining patterns.

claim: All spermatogonia within a cyst are triggered to die together even when only a subset of spermatogonia within the cyst have detectable DNA damage.
source: The above results led us to hypothesize that all SGs within a cyst might be triggered to die together even when only a subset of SGs within the cyst have detectable DNA damage, explaining the extremely high sensitivity of the germline to DNA damage.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the experimental observations of synchronized death despite heterogeneous DNA damage.

claim: The fusome is a germline-specific membranous organelle that connects the cytoplasm of germ cells within a cyst and mediates intracyst signaling amongst germ cells in Drosophila and other insects.
source: In Drosophila and other insects, the fusome is a germline-specific membranous organelle that connects the cytoplasm of germ cells within a cyst and mediates intracyst signaling amongst germ cells
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The fusome might mediate the 'all-or-none' mode of spermatogonial death upon DNA damage.
source: We speculated that if germ cell cysts undergo synchronized cell death by sharing the decision to die, the fusome might mediate the 'all-or-none' mode of SG death upon DNA damage.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the known function of the fusome in intracyst communication.

claim: α-spectrin and hts are core components of the fusome.
source: To examine the role of the fusome in all-or-none SG death upon irradiation, we used RNAi-mediated knockdown of α-spectrin and a mutant of hts, core components of the fusome
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In control testes, 16-SG cysts are almost always found to be either completely Lysotracker-positive or -negative under all conditions tested.
source: In control testes, 16-SG cysts were almost always found to be either completely Lysotracker-positive or -negative under all conditions tested as described above (Figure 3A,B,E,F)
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 3.

claim: α-spectrin RNAi and hts mutant testes frequently contain 16-SG cysts with a mixture of individual Lysotracker-positive and -negative spermatogonia.
source: In contrast, α-spectrin RNAi and hts mutant testes frequently contained 16-SG cysts with a mixture of individual Lysotracker-positive and -negative SGs (Figure 3C,D,G,H), suggesting that the all-or-none mode of SG death was compromised.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 3.

claim: The all-or-none mode of spermatogonial death is compromised in fusome mutants.
source: suggesting that the all-or-none mode of SG death was compromised.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of mixed Lysotracker staining in fusome mutant cysts.

claim: The mean fraction of 16-SG that die in response to radiation exposure at any dose is reduced when the fusome is disrupted.
source: Importantly, the mean fraction of 16-SG that died in response to radiation exposure at any dose was reduced when the fusome was disrupted (Figure 3B,D,F,H, black bars).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The fusome is required for the coordinated death of all spermatogonia within a cyst.
source: These data show that the fusome is required for the coordinated death of all SGs within a cyst, and suggests that the intracyst communication increases overall SG death in response to radiation-induced DNA damage.
evidence: This is concluded from the experimental observations in fusome mutants.

claim: Intracyst communication increases overall spermatogonial death in response to radiation-induced DNA damage.
source: and suggests that the intracyst communication increases overall SG death in response to radiation-induced DNA damage.
evidence: This is inferred from the reduced death in fusome mutants.

claim: Loss of germ cell communication in fusome mutants allows for the survival of some spermatogonia.
source: Moreover, the fact that loss of germ cell communication in fusome mutants allows for the survival of some SGs strongly argues against the possibility that SGs without cytologically detectable γ-H2Av are sufficiently damaged to trigger cell death on their own and that SGs are individually dying.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations in fusome mutants.

claim: The death of spermatogonia without detectable γ-H2Av in wild type/control can be attributed to a shared death signal from other cells.
source: Instead, the death of SGs without detectable γ-H2Av in wild type/control can likely be attributed to a shared death signal from other cells, as blockade of intercellular communication in fusome mutants allows for their survival.
evidence: This is inferred from the survival of undamaged cells in fusome mutants.

claim: Fusome mutants appear to maintain ring canals, as evidenced by the intact ring shape of Pavarotti-GFP, a marker for ring canals.
source: It should be noted that the fusome mutants appeared to maintain ring canals, as evidenced by the intact ring shape of Pavarotti-GFP, a marker for ring canals (Minestrini et al., 2002) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Intracyst communication triggering spermatogonial death is likely mediated by the fusome, rather than physical openings between spermatogonia within the cyst.
source: Therefore, intracyst communication triggering SG death is likely mediated by the fusome, rather than physical openings between SGs within the cyst (see Discussion).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that fusome mutants maintain ring canals but lose synchronized death.

claim: Somatic follicle cells of the egg chamber are connected by ring canals without a fusome.
source: Consistent with this, somatic follicle cells of the egg chamber, which are known to be connected by ring canals without a fusome (McLean and Cooley, 2013a), were observed to die individually by becoming positive for cleaved caspase (Dcp-1) (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature and experimental observations.

claim: Somatic follicle cells of the egg chamber die individually by becoming positive for cleaved caspase (Dcp-1).
source: were observed to die individually by becoming positive for cleaved caspase (Dcp-1) (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Follicle cells do not exhibit extreme sensitivity to low doses of radiation and display an essentially linear dose-response.
source: Additionally, these cells did not exhibit extreme sensitivity to low doses of radiation and displayed an essentially linear dose-response (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B,C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3B,C.

claim: Intercellular communication mediated by the fusome plays a critical role in allowing for all-or-none commitment of spermatogonia to death or survival.
source: The above results suggest that intercellular communication mediated by the fusome plays a critical role in allowing for all-or-none commitment of SGs to death or survival.
evidence: This is concluded from the experimental observations in fusome mutants.

claim: A signal to promote cell death exists that is rapidly transmitted from damaged spermatogonia to others via their intercellular connections.
source: Based on these results, we hypothesized that a signal to promote cell death exists that is rapidly transmitted from damaged SGs to others via their intercellular connections.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the experimental observations.

claim: Germ cell death in the Drosophila testis is non-apoptotic and depends on mitochondria-associated factors.
source: It has previously been shown that germ cell death in the Drosophila testis is non-apoptotic, and depends on mitochondria-associated factors (Yacobi-Sharon et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The Drosophila homolog of the mitochondrial serine protease HtrA2/Omi is cleaved and released from the mitochondrial compartment as part of the mitochondria-associated death pathway to promote cell death in response to nuclear DNA damage.
source: The Drosophila homolog of the mitochondrial serine protease HtrA2/Omi is cleaved and released from the mitochondrial compartment as part of the mitochondria-associated death pathway to promote cell death in response to nuclear DNA damage
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The catalytic function of released HtrA2/Omi is known to control the death of spermatogonia in the testis.
source: The catalytic function of released HtrA2/Omi is known to control the death of SGs in the testis.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Endonuclease G (EndoG) is involved in germ cell death.
source: Yacobi-Sharon et al. further showed that Endonuclease G (EndoG) is also involved in germ cell death (Yacobi-Sharon et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: EndoG normally resides in mitochondria but is released to promote degradation of nuclear chromatin and induce cell death.
source: EndoG normally resides in mitochondria but is released to promote degradation of nuclear chromatin and induce cell death (Widlak and Garrard, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: In HtrA2/Omi mutant flies, a mix of Lysotracker-positive and -negative spermatogonia is frequently observed within a single cyst.
source: In HtrA2/Omi mutant flies, we frequently observed a mix of Lysotracker-positive and -negative SGs within a single cyst, similar to what was seen in fusome mutants (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Disruption of the all-or-none mode of spermatogonial death within the cyst occurs at any dose of radiation tested in HtrA2/Omi mutants.
source: Disruption of the all-or-none mode of SG death within the cyst was observed at any dose of radiation tested (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Disrupted all-or-none spermatogonial death occurs in both heterozygous (OmiΔ1/+) and transheterozygous (OmiΔ1/OmiDf1) conditions.
source: Disrupted all-or-none SG death occurred in both heterozygous (OmiΔ1/+) and transheterozygous (OmiΔ1/OmiDf1) conditions, consistent with the previous report that heterozygous conditions exhibit haploinsufficiency in inducing SG death
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations and a citation to prior literature.

claim: Heterozygous HtrA2/Omi conditions exhibit haploinsufficiency in inducing spermatogonial death.
source: consistent with the previous report that heterozygous conditions exhibit haploinsufficiency in inducing SG death (Yacobi-Sharon et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Wild type control 16-SG cysts maintain their all-or-none mode of spermatogonial death.
source: In contrast, wild type control 16-SG cysts maintained their all-or-none mode of SG death (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 4B.

claim: A loss-of-function EndoGMB07150 mutant allele shows disruption of all-or-none spermatogonial death in both heterozygous (EndoGMB07150/+) and transheterozygous (EndoGMB07150/Df(3R)BSC699) conditions.
source: Likewise, a loss-of-function EndoGMB07150 mutant allele (DeLuca and O'Farrell, 2012) also showed disruption of all-or-none SG death in both heterozygous (EndoGMB07150/+) and transheterozygous (EndoGMB07150/Df(3R)BSC699) conditions (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 4C,D.

claim: Mitochondrial cell death pathway components HtrA2/Omi and EndoG are involved in the all-or-none mode of spermatogonial death.
source: Taken together, these data show the involvement of mitochondrial cell death pathway components HtrA2/Omi and EndoG in the all-or-none mode of SG death.
evidence: This is concluded from the experimental observations in HtrA2/Omi and EndoG mutants.

claim: HtrA2/Omi and EndoG or their downstream molecules/signals may be shared among spermatogonia via the fusome to trigger synchronized spermatogonial death.
source: Considering that these proteins are released from mitochondria to induce cell death, it is tempting to speculate that these proteins (or their downstream molecules/signals) are shared among SGs via the fusome to trigger synchronized SG death.
evidence: This is speculation based on the known functions of these proteins and the experimental observations.

claim: The DNA damage response is a highly conserved pathway controlling cell death and DNA repair.
source: The DNA damage response is a highly conserved pathway controlling cell death and DNA repair (Ciccia and Elledge, 2010; Song, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: mnk/chk2 and p53 have conserved function in DNA damage response in Drosophila.
source: We thus examined the potential involvement in radiation-induced SG death of the universal DNA damage response pathway components, mnk/chk2 and p53, whose conserved function in DNA damage response in Drosophila has been shown
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: mnk/chk2 and p53 mutants broadly suppress spermatogonial death at high and low doses of radiation.
source: By using well-characterized loss-of-function alleles (mnk6006 and p535A-1-4) (Takada et al., 2003; Wichmann et al., 2006; Xie and Golic, 2004), we found that these mutants broadly suppress SG death at high and low doses of radiation (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Spermatogonial death in mnk/chk2 and p53 mutants maintains an all-or-none pattern.
source: However, SG death in these mutants maintained an all-or-none pattern (Figure 5A–C,E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 5.

claim: p53 and mnk/chk2 may contribute to spermatogonial death via their general role in controlling the DNA damage response.
source: These results suggest that while p53 and mnk/chk2 may contribute to SG death via their general role in controlling the DNA damage response as has been described in somatic cells, they do not play a role in mediating the all-or-none pattern of SG death within a cyst that is unique to interconnected germ cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that these mutants suppress death but maintain all-or-none pattern.

claim: p53 and mnk/chk2 do not play a role in mediating the all-or-none pattern of spermatogonial death within a cyst that is unique to interconnected germ cells.
source: they do not play a role in mediating the all-or-none pattern of SG death within a cyst that is unique to interconnected germ cells.
evidence: This is concluded from the observation that these mutants maintain all-or-none death pattern.

claim: Mnk/Chk2 or p53 is barely upregulated in the germline in response to a low dose of radiation (100 rad).
source: Consistent with the idea that neither mnk/chk2 or p53 is responsible for a germline-specific, all-or-none mode of cell death in response to DNA damage, Mnk/Chk2 or p53 was barely upregulated in the germline in response to a low dose of radiation (100 rad), which is sufficient to induce robust SG death.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations using antibody staining and reporter assays.

claim: Mnk/Chk2 is barely detected in germ cells, although some level of signal is seen in the surrounding somatic cyst cells.
source: Using a polyclonal anti-Mnk/Chk2 antibody (Takada et al., 2015), we barely detected any signal in germ cells, although some level of signal was seen in the surrounding somatic cyst cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: A p53 transcriptional reporter shows only a slight increase in signal in response to a low dose of radiation.
source: Likewise, a p53 transcriptional reporter (Wylie et al., 2014) showed only a slight increase in the signal in response to a low dose of radiation (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: At a high dose of radiation, robust expression of the p53 reporter is observed only at 24 hr after irradiation, much later than the peak of spermatogonial death.
source: Even at a high dose, robust expression of the reporter was observed only at 24 hr after irradiation, much later than the peak of SG death, which typically happens within a few hours.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations.

claim: Expression of p53 or Mnk/Chk2 in spermatogonia is unlikely to account for the all-or-none mode of germ cell death in response to DNA damage.
source: Collectively, these data (i.e. mnk/chk2 and p53 mutants maintaining all-or-none cell death and the lack of robust Mnk/Chk2 and p53 expression in response to DNA damage) indicate that expression of p53 or Mnk/Chk2 in SGs is unlikely to account for the all-or-none mode of germ cell death in response to DNA damage.
evidence: This is concluded from the experimental observations on mnk/chk2 and p53 mutants and expression patterns.

claim: The ability of spermatogonia to trigger cell death in response to DNA damage is facilitated by the sharing of death-promoting signals amongst spermatogonia within a cyst.
source: The above results suggest that the ability of SGs to trigger cell death in response to DNA damage is facilitated by the sharing of death-promoting signals amongst SGs within a cyst, killing SGs that are not sufficiently damaged to commit to cell death on their own.
evidence: This is concluded from all the experimental observations.

claim: Sharing of death-promoting signals kills spermatogonia that are not sufficiently damaged to commit to cell death on their own.
source: killing SGs that are not sufficiently damaged to commit to cell death on their own.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that undamaged cells die in wild type but survive in fusome mutants.

claim: Sharing of death-promoting signals is mediated by and dependent on the fusome, which facilitates intracyst communication.
source: This sharing of death-promoting signals is mediated by and dependent on the fusome, which facilitates intracyst communication.
evidence: This is concluded from the experimental observations in fusome mutants.

claim: Increasing the connectivity of a spermatogonial cyst (the number of interconnected spermatogonia within the cyst) would increase its sensitivity to DNA damage.
source: If this is the case, it would be predicted that increasing the connectivity of a SG cyst (the number of interconnected SGs within the cyst) would increase its sensitivity to DNA damage, because increased SG number per cyst will increase the probability of any cells being sufficiently damaged to trigger death.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the model of shared death signals.

claim: 16-SG cysts die more frequently than 2-, 4-, or 8-SGs.
source: Indeed, as mentioned above, we observed a trend of 16-SG cysts dying more frequently than 2-, 4-, or 8-SGs (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The sensitivity of spermatogonial cysts correlates with their connectivity, where 8-SGs are less sensitive than 16-SGs but more sensitive than 4-SGs.
source: By plotting cell death frequency of all SG stages as a function of increasing radiation dose (Figure 6A), it becomes clear that the sensitivity of SG cysts correlates with their connectivity, where 8-SGs are less sensitive than 16-SGs but more sensitive than 4-SGs and so on.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Single-celled gonialblasts, the immediate daughter of germline stem cells that have not formed any intercellular connections, exhibit an essentially linear increase in death in response to radiation dose.
source: Interestingly, single-celled GBs, the immediate daughter of GSCs that have not formed any intercellular connections, exhibited an essentially linear increase in death in response to radiation dose, which is reminiscent of somatic imaginal disc cells or follicle cells (Figure 1D, Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Germ cell connectivity plays a key role in increasing the sensitivity of the germline to DNA damage.
source: These results support the idea that germ cell connectivity plays a key role in increasing the sensitivity of the germline to DNA damage.
evidence: This is concluded from the correlation between connectivity and sensitivity to DNA damage.

claim: The connectivity of germ cells can serve as a key mechanism for their ability to robustly induce cell death.
source: Our study in the Drosophila male germline shows that the connectivity of germ cells can serve as a key mechanism for their ability to robustly induce cell death, providing an explanation for cyst formation outside of the oocyte nursing mechanism.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: Early-stage embryos of Drosophila develop as syncytia, where all nuclei are within a connected cytoplasm.
source: For example, early-stage embryos of Drosophila develop as syncytia, where all nuclei are within a connected cytoplasm.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila development.

claim: The C. elegans germline is topologically similar to Drosophila early embryos in that all cells share the same cytoplasm.
source: The C. elegans germline is topologically similar to Drosophila early embryos in that all cells share the same cytoplasm.
evidence: This is established knowledge about C. elegans germline.

claim: In Drosophila early embryos and C. elegans germline, damaged nuclei die individually and synchronized cell death is not observed.
source: In these two examples, damaged nuclei die individually and synchronized cell death is not observed (Lettre et al., 2004; Takada et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In Drosophila oogenesis, 16 interconnected cystocytes have distinct fates (one oocyte and 15 nurse cells).
source: In Drosophila oogenesis, 16 interconnected cystocytes have distinct fates (one oocyte and 15 nurse cells), and it would not be beneficial to kill the oocyte when just one dispensable nurse cell is damaged.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila oogenesis.

claim: Nurse cells undergo programmed apoptosis later in oogenesis to finalize the cytoplasmic transport into the oocyte, yet this apoptosis does not kill oocytes.
source: Moreover, nurse cells undergo programmed apoptosis later in oogenesis to finalize the cytoplasmic transport into the oocyte, yet this apoptosis does not kill oocytes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila oogenesis.

claim: Openness via ring canals/intercellular bridges alone is likely insufficient to mediate synchronized cell death.
source: These examples have two important implications. First, openness via ring canals/intercellular bridges alone is likely insufficient to mediate synchronized cell death.
evidence: This is inferred from the examples where connected cells do not exhibit synchronized death.

claim: There are likely additional purposes for intercellular connectivity to be discovered other than the sharing of death-promoting signals.
source: Second, there are likely additional purposes for intercellular connectivity to be discovered other than the sharing of death-promoting signals.
evidence: This is speculation based on the diverse contexts of intercellular connectivity.

claim: The fusome plays a key role in facilitating intercellular communication of death-promoting signals.
source: Regarding the first point that physical openness alone is likely insufficient to induce cell death in undamaged sibling cells, we speculate that the fusome plays a key role in facilitating intercellular communication of death-promoting signals.
evidence: This is speculation based on the experimental observations in fusome mutants.

claim: Fusome mutants apparently maintain cytoplasmic openings (ring canals) between spermatogonia.
source: Because fusome mutants apparently maintain cytoplasmic openings (ring canals) between SGs (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), it suggests that the intercellular bridges/openings are not sufficient to allow intracyst communication of death-promoting signals.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Intercellular bridges/openings are not sufficient to allow intracyst communication of death-promoting signals.
source: it suggests that the intercellular bridges/openings are not sufficient to allow intracyst communication of death-promoting signals.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that fusome mutants maintain ring canals but lose synchronized death.

claim: Follicle cells of the egg chamber are known to maintain intercellular bridges/ring canals among multiple sibling cells, through which molecules (e.g. GFP) can be transported.
source: Consistent with this idea, we found that follicle cells of the egg chamber do not exhibit synchronized cell death in response to irradiation (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A), even though these cells are known to maintain intercellular bridges/ring canals among multiple sibling cells, through which molecules (e.g. GFP) can be transported (McLean and Cooley, 2013a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The fusome functions to transmit the death-triggering signals, similar to its known role in cell cycle synchronization within the germ cell cyst.
source: Therefore, we propose that the fusome functions to transmit the death-triggering signals, similar to its known role in cell cycle synchronization within the germ cell cyst (Lilly et al., 2000)(Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a proposal based on the experimental observations and known fusome function.

claim: When one spermatogonium within a cyst decides to die, this 'decision of death' might be sent to all the other spermatogonia within the cyst, leading to all-or-none spermatogonial death.
source: We imagine two possibilities to explain how the signals are shared within a cyst, leading to cell death: when one SG within a cyst decides to die, this 'decision of death' might be sent to all the other SGs within the cyst, leading to all-or-none SG death.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism of signal sharing.

claim: The signal shared among spermatogonia may be 'additive' in nature, where addition of all damage signaling within the cyst might reach a level sufficient to induce cell death even when none of the individual spermatogonia have sufficient DNA damage to trigger cell death on its own.
source: Alternatively, the signal shared among SGs may be 'additive' in nature. In such a scenario, even when none of the individual SGs have sufficient DNA damage to trigger cell death on its own, addition of all damage signaling within the cyst might reach a level sufficient to induce cell death.
evidence: This is speculation about an alternative mechanism of signal sharing.

claim: Sharing of signals between spermatogonia through intercellular connections would effectively lower the threshold of DNA damage per cell needed to trigger germ cell death.
source: Either way, such responses would effectively lower the threshold of DNA damage per cell needed to trigger germ cell death.
evidence: This is inferred from the proposed mechanisms of signal sharing.

claim: The sharing of signals between spermatogonia through intercellular connections increases their likelihood to die following DNA damage, explaining the unusually high sensitivity of the germline to DNA damage.
source: Consequently, the sharing of signals between SGs through intercellular connections increases their likelihood to die following DNA damage, explaining the unusually high sensitivity of the germline to DNA damage.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: Higher connectivity confers higher sensitivity to DNA damage: as the connectivity increases, more cells would contribute to detecting any DNA damage the germline may be experiencing.
source: According to this model, higher connectivity would confer higher sensitivity to DNA damage: as the connectivity increases, more cells would contribute to detecting any DNA damage the germline may be experiencing.
evidence: This is inferred from the model of shared death signals.

claim: Individual germ cells do not necessarily have an intrinsically different DNA damage response that accounts for their high sensitivity to DNA damage.
source: Remarkably, the fact that single-celled, unconnected GBs exhibit an essentially linear death response to increasing radiation suggests that individual germ cells do not necessarily have an intrinsically different DNA damage response that accounts for their high sensitivity to DNA damage (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that unconnected germ cells behave like somatic cells.

claim: A connectivity-based increase in sensitivity to DNA damage has an important implication in the development of multicellular organisms.
source: A connectivity-based increase in sensitivity to DNA damage also has an important implication in the development of multicellular organisms.
evidence: This is speculation about the broader implications of the findings.

claim: It is critically important for germ cells to have the most stringent mechanisms to prevent deleterious mutations.
source: To pass on genomes to the next generation, it is critically important for germ cells to have the most stringent mechanisms to prevent deleterious mutations.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the importance of genome integrity in the germline.

claim: As genome size increases in multicellular organisms, ubiquitously increasing the stringency of genome quality control could result in a high rate of cell death in all tissues, which could compromise the development or survival of organisms.
source: However, as genome size increases in multicellular organisms, ubiquitously increasing the stringency of genome quality control could result in a high rate of cell death in all tissues, which could compromise the development or survival of organisms.
evidence: This is speculation about the evolutionary constraints on genome quality control.

claim: A multicellular organism may require differential sensitivities to DNA damage between the soma and the germline: a more sensitive genome surveillance mechanism to protect the germline, whereas the priority of the soma shifts toward survival to support development/maintenance of somatic organs.
source: Thus, a multicellular organism may require differential sensitivities to DNA damage between the soma and the germline: a more sensitive genome surveillance mechanism to protect the germline, whereas the priority of the soma shifting toward survival to support development/maintenance of somatic organs.
evidence: This is speculation about the evolutionary rationale for differential DNA damage sensitivity.

claim: A connectivity-based increase in sensitivity to DNA damage might be a simple method for multicellular organisms to achieve drastically different sensitivities to DNA damage between the soma and germline without having to alter intrinsic damage response pathways.
source: A connectivity-based increase in sensitivity to DNA damage might be a simple method for multicellular organisms to achieve drastically different sensitivities to DNA damage between the soma and germline without having to alter intrinsic damage response pathways, although additional germline-specific DNA damage response mechanisms cannot be excluded.
evidence: This is speculation about the evolutionary advantage of connectivity-based sensitivity.

claim: One reason germ cell connectivity has arisen during evolution and been so widely conserved might be to confer higher sensitivity to DNA damage specifically in the germline.
source: We speculate that one reason germ cell connectivity has arisen during evolution and been so widely conserved might be to confer higher sensitivity to DNA damage specifically in the germline.
evidence: This is speculation about the evolutionary origin and conservation of germ cell connectivity.
